title: Sweetheart Roland
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a woman who was a real witch and had two daughters. One was ugly and wicked, and she loved this one because she was her own daughter. The other was beautiful and good, and she hated this one because she was her stepdaughter. The stepdaughter once had a pretty apron, and the other girl liked it so much that she grew jealous and told her mother she must and would have that apron. “Hush, my child,” said the old woman, “you’ll have it. Your stepsister has deserved to die for a long time. Tonight, when she’s asleep, I’ll come and cut her head off. Just make sure you lie on the far side of the bed, and push her well to the front.” It would have been the end of the poor girl if she hadn’t been standing in a corner at that moment and heard every word. She didn’t dare leave the house all day, and when bedtime came, the witch’s daughter got into bed first, to lie on the far side. But once she was asleep, the other girl gently pushed her to the front and took the place at the back for herself, next to the wall. In the night the old woman came creeping in, an axe in her right hand, feeling with her left to check whether someone was lying on the outside. Then she gripped the axe with both hands and cut off her own child’s head.

When the witch had gone, the girl got up, went to her sweetheart, whose name was Roland, and knocked on his door. When he came out, she said to him, “Listen, dearest Roland, we have to flee at once. My stepmother wanted to kill me, but she has struck down her own child. When daylight comes and she sees what she’s done, we’ll be lost.” “But,” said Roland, “my advice is to take her magic wand first, or we can’t get away if she chases us.” The girl fetched the magic wand. Then she took the dead girl’s head and let three drops of blood fall on the ground, one in front of the bed, one in the kitchen and one on the stairs. Then she hurried off with her lover.

When the old witch got up the next morning, she called her daughter, meaning to give her the apron, but the girl didn’t come. So the witch cried, “Where are you?” “Here on the stairs, sweeping,” answered the first drop of blood. The old woman went out but saw no one on the stairs, and called again, “Where are you?” “Here in the kitchen, warming myself,” called the second drop of blood. She went into the kitchen but found no one. Then she called again, “Where are you?” “Ah, here in the bed, sleeping,” called the third drop of blood. She went into the room, up to the bed. What did she see? Her own child, whose head she had cut off, lying in her blood. The witch flew into a rage and sprang to the window, and since she could see a long way out over the world, she spotted her stepdaughter hurrying off with her sweetheart Roland. “That won’t save you,” she cried. “Even if you’ve gone a long way, you still won’t escape me.” She pulled on her many-league boots, which covered an hour’s walk with every step, and it wasn’t long before she caught up with them. But when the girl saw the old woman striding toward her, she used her magic wand to turn her sweetheart Roland into a lake and herself into a duck swimming in the middle of it. The witch stood on the shore, threw breadcrumbs in and went to endless trouble to lure the duck, but the duck wouldn’t be lured, and the old woman had to go home at nightfall just as she had come. Then the girl and her sweetheart Roland took their own shapes again, and they walked all night until daybreak. Then the girl turned herself into a beautiful flower growing in the middle of a briar hedge, and her sweetheart Roland into a fiddler. It wasn’t long before the witch came striding up and said to the musician, “Dear musician, may I pick that beautiful flower for myself?” “Oh yes,” he replied, “and I’ll play for you while you do it.” She was hurriedly creeping into the hedge and was just about to pluck the flower, knowing perfectly well who the flower was, when he began to play. Whether she wanted to or not, she was forced to dance, for it was a magic dance. The faster he played, the wilder the leaps she had to make, and the thorns tore the clothes from her body and pricked and wounded her until she bled. Since he never stopped, she had to dance until she lay dead on the ground.

Now that they were free, Roland said, “I’ll go to my father and arrange the wedding.” “Then I’ll stay here and wait for you,” said the girl, “and so that nobody recognizes me, I’ll turn myself into a red boundary stone.” So Roland left, and the girl stood in the field as a red boundary stone, waiting for her beloved. But when Roland reached home, he fell into another woman’s trap. She bewitched him so completely that he forgot the girl. The poor girl stayed there a long time, but in the end, when he never came back, she grew sad and turned herself into a flower, thinking, “Somebody is sure to walk by and trample me.”

It happened, though, that a shepherd was grazing his sheep in that field. He noticed the flower, and because it was so pretty he picked it, took it home and put it away in his chest. From then on, strange things went on in the shepherd’s house. Every morning when he got up, all the work was already finished: the room was swept, the table and benches were wiped clean, the fire was burning in the hearth, and the water was fetched. At noon, when he came home, the table was set and a good dinner was waiting. He could not understand how this came about, since he never saw a soul in his house, and nobody could have hidden in it. He was pleased enough with such good service, but in the end he grew so frightened that he went to a wise woman and asked her advice. The wise woman said, “There is some enchantment behind this. Some morning, listen very early for anything stirring in the room, and if you see something, whatever it is, throw a white cloth over it, and the magic will be broken.”

The shepherd did as she told him. The next morning, just as day was breaking, he saw the chest open and the flower step out. He leapt toward it quickly and threw a white cloth over it. At once the spell ended, and a beautiful girl stood in front of him. She told him she had been the flower and that until now she had been looking after his house. She told him her story, and since he liked her, he asked whether she would marry him. But she said “No,” because she wanted to stay true to her sweetheart Roland, even though he had abandoned her. Even so, she promised not to leave, and to go on keeping house for the shepherd.

Now the time came near for Roland’s wedding. According to an old custom of the country, it was proclaimed that all the girls must attend and sing in honor of the bride and groom. When the faithful girl heard this, she became so sad that she thought her heart would break, and she did not want to go there, but the other girls came and fetched her. When her turn to sing came, she kept stepping back until she was the only one left, and then she could not refuse. But as soon as she began her song and it reached Roland’s ears, he jumped up and cried, “I know that voice! That is the true bride, and I will have no other!” Everything he had forgotten, everything that had slipped from his mind, suddenly came back to his heart. Then the faithful girl married her sweetheart Roland, and sorrow ended and joy began.
